source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: A simple model gives the chance a claimed finding is true (PPV) from power, the 0.05 threshold, and the prior ratio of true to false relationships R.
numbers: PPV = (1-beta)R/(R - beta R + alpha). A finding is more likely true than false only if (1-beta)R > alpha (about 0.05).
limits: Model only. R and the bias term are assumed, not measured. Not an empirical count of false papers.
agent_relevance: Gives the arithmetic for G3: one fitted pass is weak evidence when priors are low. A held-out check raises PPV.

source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: Six corollaries: small studies, small effects, many tested relationships, flexible designs, financial or other interests, and hot fields all lower the chance a finding is true.
numbers: Corollaries 1 to 6 as listed. Corollary 6: more teams chasing significance lowers the PPV of each isolated finding.
quote: The hotter a scientific field (with more scientific teams involved), the less likely the research findings are to be true.
limits: Derived from the model. Later empirical work (OSC, Camerer) supports the direction but not the exact size.
agent_relevance: An agent that tries many candidate answers against few examples is in the 'many tested relationships, flexible design' regime. Fit alone proves little.

source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: Table 4 simulations: PPV depends strongly on design. Confirmatory trials are mostly true; exploratory and massive-testing work is mostly false.
numbers: Adequately powered RCT with 50% prior: true about 85% of the time. Underpowered early-phase trial: about 1 in 4. Well-powered exploratory epidemiology at R=1:10: about 1 in 5. Massive testing (30,000 genes, 30 true): PPV extremely low.
limits: Simulated values under assumed bias settings.
agent_relevance: Rank checks by design: a held-out confirmatory test is worth far more than another fit on the training set.

source: Serra-Garcia and Gneezy (2021) Nonreplicable publications are cited more than replicable ones
finding: Papers that failed replication in three large projects are cited more, and the gap does not shrink after the failed replication is published.
numbers: Failed papers cited about 16 more times per year (random-effects Poisson, P=0.005). In the Nature/Science sample (N=80), papers that replicate are cited 153 fewer times in total.
quote: Published papers that fail to replicate are cited more than those that replicate, even after the failure is published.
limits: Citation counts are observational. Samples are the studies picked by the three replication projects (psychology, economics, Nature/Science).
agent_relevance: Contradicted results persist. An agent that retrieves literature or past notes should weight a recorded failed check above citation count or popularity.

source: Serra-Garcia and Gneezy (2021) Nonreplicable publications are cited more than replicable ones
finding: Only a small share of later citations of a non-replicable paper mention the failure.
numbers: Only 12% of post-replication citations of nonreplicable findings acknowledge the replication failure.
limits: Coded from citing texts in the study sample; coding scheme is the authors'.
agent_relevance: Store a failed check next to the claim in memory, or it will be dropped.

source: Serra-Garcia and Gneezy (2021) Nonreplicable publications are cited more than replicable ones
finding: The paper restates the founding replication-project numbers it builds on (Open Science Collaboration 2015; Camerer et al. 2016, 2018).
numbers: Psychology: 39% of replications significant vs 97% of originals. Economics: 61% of 18 studies replicated. Nature/Science: 62% of 21 replicated. Replicated effects were about 75% of original size; failed ones close to 0%.
limits: Second-hand summary. The original OSC and Camerer papers were paywalled and not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Effect-size shrinkage (about 25% even among successes) is a reason to discount any single positive result.

source: Serra-Garcia and Gneezy (2021) Nonreplicable publications are cited more than replicable ones
finding: They propose reviewers trade off interest against rigor: more interesting results get lower reproducibility standards. Experts predict replication well, yet such papers still get published.
numbers: Prediction markets and surveys predicted replication well (cited from earlier work).
quote: When the results are more interesting, they apply lower standards regarding their reproducibility.
limits: A proposed explanation; not directly tested against reviewer behaviour here.
agent_relevance: The agent's pull toward an 'interesting' answer may lower its checking bar. Fix the check bar in code (G5), not by how exciting the answer looks.

source: Greenberg (2009) How citation distortions create unfounded authority
finding: A full citation network on one claim (beta amyloid in inclusion body myositis) shows how a belief gets authority without evidence.
numbers: Network: 242 papers, 675 citations, 220,553 citation paths supporting the claim. Mechanisms named: citation bias, amplification, invention.
quote: Citation is both an impartial scholarly method and a powerful form of social communication.
limits: One claim case study. NIH grant texts obtained via FOIA showed the same pattern.
agent_relevance: Repeated citation is not independent confirmation (G4). Count independent evidence sources, not mentions.

source: Greenberg (2009) How citation distortions create unfounded authority
finding: Citation bias and amplification: critical primary data were ignored while support grew with little new data.
numbers: Between 1996 and 2007 supportive citations grew sevenfold (to 636) and supportive paths 777-fold; the critical view reached only 21 citations and 28 paths. Of the 10 most authoritative papers, 4 had data, all from one lab.
quote: No papers refuted or critiqued the critical data, but instead the data were just ignored.
limits: Network is from one subfield. Counts depend on the authors' claim coding.
agent_relevance: Contradicting evidence is dropped by silence, not rebuttal. Force the agent to list disconfirming evidence before it settles.

source: Greenberg (2009) How citation distortions create unfounded authority
finding: Invention: a hypothesis was turned into fact by citation alone (for example, early amyloid accumulation preceding other abnormalities).
numbers: Subclaim restated variously as hypothesis, likelihood, or fact across the network.
limits: Qualitative classification.
agent_relevance: Track status labels (hypothesis vs tested) per claim; do not let a restated claim upgrade itself.

source: Smaldino and McElreath (2016) The natural selection of bad science
finding: A 60-year review of statistical power in behavioral science finds low power with no trend.
numbers: Mean power to detect small effects (d=0.2) was 0.24, so such effects are missed three times in four. No increase over six decades (R squared = 0.00097).
limits: Uses earlier power surveys (Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer 1989, Rossi 1990, plus new data); small effect assumed d=0.2.
agent_relevance: Peer review did not screen out underpowered work. A pass from a weak test (few examples) is cheap and common.

source: Smaldino and McElreath (2016) The natural selection of bad science
finding: Agent-based model of competing labs with copied methods: selection for publication output drives power and false positive rate up and effort down.
numbers: Without replication, power and false positive rate both go to 1 and the false discovery rate rises. Output counts, not truth, set fitness.
quote: Selection for high output leads to poorer methods and increasingly high false discovery rates.
limits: Stylized model, 'illustrative rather than exploratory'; payoffs set by the authors.
agent_relevance: Any selection loop scored on output volume degrades quality. Score the chooser on held-out truth, not on count of passes.

source: Smaldino and McElreath (2016) The natural selection of bad science
finding: Replication slows but does not stop methodological decline in the model.
numbers: Evolved mean replication rate settled near 0.08. With replication forced to 25% or 50% of all studies, effort still fell to its floor, only later. A positive replication paid half a novel result.
quote: Replication is not sufficient to curb the natural selection of bad science.
limits: Assumptions are favourable to replication. Authors do not endorse punitive payoffs.
agent_relevance: Replication alone is not enough. Pair it with a fixed cost for skipped checks and checks chosen by code.

source: Cortes and Lawrence (2021) Inconsistency in conference peer review: revisiting the 2014 NeurIPS experiment
finding: Two independent committees reviewed the same 10% of NeurIPS 2014 papers. Decisions often disagreed.
numbers: 166 papers completed. Committees disagreed on 43 papers (25.0%). Of 43 accepted by committee 1, committee 2 accepted 22 (51%); of 44 accepted by committee 2, committee 1 accepted 22 (50%). Score correlation r=0.55 (SE 0.065). Accept rate about 23%.
limits: Single conference, one year, small N. Accept-consistency estimates are imprecise (38% to 64% in an appendix).
agent_relevance: Peer review is a noisy judge. One judge's pass near the margin is close to a coin flip; supports code-side held-out checks over model self-grading.

source: Cortes and Lawrence (2021) Inconsistency in conference peer review: revisiting the 2014 NeurIPS experiment
finding: A calibration model splits reviewer score variance into shared and reviewer-specific parts.
numbers: About 50% of a typical reviewer's calibrated score is subjective. Model-implied committee correlation 0.50 (1.28/(1.28+1.27)) vs observed 0.55. With 3 reviewers and 50% subjectivity, simulated accept consistency is about 63%, above the observed value.
quote: 50% of the variation in reviewer quality scores was subjective in origin.
limits: Model fit is partial; it over-predicts accept consistency.
agent_relevance: Independent judges carry half private noise, so averaging helps only to a limit. Judges from one model share even more error (G4).

source: Cortes and Lawrence (2021) Inconsistency in conference peer review: revisiting the 2014 NeurIPS experiment
finding: Seven years later, review scores did not predict impact among accepted papers, but did among rejected ones.
numbers: About 400 accepted papers: no correlation of quality score with citations. 680 rejected papers tracked to their final outlet: score correlated with citations.
quote: Reviewing was good for identifying poor papers, but poor for identifying good papers.
limits: Citations are a proxy for impact. Rejected-paper matching used title and author search.
agent_relevance: Filters are better at removing bad candidates than ranking good ones. Use checks to veto, not to rank survivors.

source: Pier et al. (2018) Low agreement among reviewers evaluating the same NIH grant applications
finding: 43 reviewers rated the same 25 NIH applications under a replicated NIH process and showed no agreement.
numbers: 43 reviewers, 25 applications. No agreement in quantitative or qualitative evaluations; no agreement on how strengths and weaknesses map to a number.
quote: The outcome of the grant review depended more on the reviewer to whom the grant was assigned than the research proposed.
limits: Abstract only (via Europe PMC); full text not opened. Small simulated panel.
agent_relevance: Reviewer identity can matter more than content. A single LLM judge is one such reviewer.

source: Gilbert et al. (2016) Comment on 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science' and response
finding: Gilbert et al. argued the 100-study project shows high reproducibility given sampling error; the project authors answered that both optimistic and pessimistic readings fit the data.
numbers: Abstracts only. No numbers read this session.
quote: Both optimistic and pessimistic conclusions about reproducibility are possible, and neither are yet warranted.
limits: Abstract only. Replication success depends on the criterion chosen (significance, effect-size overlap, meta-analysis).
agent_relevance: Pick the pass criterion before the run and fix it in code; otherwise 'it replicated' can be argued either way.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Can large language models provide useful feedback on research papers?
finding: GPT-4 review points overlap human review points about as much as two humans overlap each other.
numbers: Nature family: 3,096 papers (8,745 human comments); ICLR: 1,709 papers (6,505 comments). GPT-4 vs human overlap 30.85% (Nature) and 39.23% (ICLR); human vs human 28.58% and 35.25%. Rejected ICLR papers: GPT-4 overlap 43.80%.
limits: Overlap judged by an LLM matching pipeline (F1 96.8% extraction, 82.4% matching). Overlap is not correctness.
agent_relevance: LLM feedback finds the common points; humans miss the same points, so overlap does not show the review is right.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Can large language models provide useful feedback on research papers?
finding: Researchers rated GPT-4 feedback on their own papers as useful.
numbers: 308 researchers from 110 US institutions. 57.4% found it helpful or very helpful; 82.4% found it more beneficial than feedback from at least some human reviewers.
limits: Self-reported, AI and computational biology fields. Authors list limits such as generic comments.
agent_relevance: LLM critique is a fair source of candidate issues but still needs code-side verification (G2).

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Blind expert review found LLM ideas more novel than human expert ideas.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition. 79 reviewers, 104 participants in all. Novelty mean: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p<0.05). AI ideas comparable on feasibility.
quote: LLM-generated ideas are judged as more novel (p < 0.05) than human expert ideas.
limits: Judged, not executed. One field (NLP prompting topics). Authors note novelty judgments are hard even for experts.
agent_relevance: Novelty here is only a reviewer opinion, the same noisy signal the review studies above show.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Reviewer agreement on ideas was only modestly above chance.
numbers: Split-half agreement on top/bottom 25% of ideas: 56.1%. NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment, same metric: 66.0%. ICLR 2024 LM-related submissions: 71.9%.
limits: Split-half metric with small samples per idea.
agent_relevance: Expert panels agree barely better than half; settle ideas with executed held-out results.

source: Ye et al. (2024) Are we there yet? Revealing the risks of utilizing large language models in scholarly peer review
finding: Covert text in a manuscript can steer LLM reviews almost completely.
numbers: Explicit manipulation raised agreement with injected content to 90% and cut agreement with human reviews from 53% to 16%. Average rating moved from 5.34 to 7.99. Simulation: manipulating 5% of reviews could push 12% of papers out of the top 30%.
limits: ICLR-style data with a rating model; simulation assumptions are the authors'.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge is attackable by the text it judges. A judge reading the candidate's own argument inherits its framing (G5).

source: Ye et al. (2024) Are we there yet? Revealing the risks of utilizing large language models in scholarly peer review
finding: LLM reviewers echo author-disclosed limitations, rate incomplete papers high, and favour famous authors in single-blind mode.
numbers: LLM reviews 4.5 times more consistent with authors' stated limitations than human reviews. Title-only papers scored higher or equal to 42% of full papers on average. Naming well-known authors gave more favourable review content.
limits: Controlled manipulations, not a field audit.
agent_relevance: Hide authorship and proposed answers from any model judge. Check for length or completeness effects.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: evaluating AI's ability to replicate AI research
finding: Agents must rebuild 20 ICML 2024 papers from scratch and are graded on a rubric tree.
numbers: 20 papers, 8,316 gradable outcomes, rubrics co-written with original authors. Best agent (Claude 3.5 Sonnet New, simple scaffold): 21.0% replication score.
limits: Scores are rubric-weighted and graded by an LLM judge; ML papers only.
agent_relevance: Agents are far from replicating published results. Do not trust a claim of reproduction without an actual run.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: evaluating AI's ability to replicate AI research
finding: Humans beat the model on a 3-paper subset; judge quality was measured.
numbers: ML PhDs, best of 3, 48 hours: 41.4% vs 26.6% for o1 on the same subset. PaperBench Code-Dev: o1 43.4%. Best LLM judge (o3-mini-high with scaffolding) F1 0.83 vs human gold labels.
limits: Human baseline is only 3 papers.
agent_relevance: An LLM grader at F1 0.83 is a usable stand-in, but keep code-run checks as the final gate.

source: Siegel et al. (2024) CORE-Bench: fostering the credibility of published research through a computational reproducibility agent benchmark
finding: Benchmark of 270 tasks from 90 papers in CS, social science and medicine; agents must run the authors' code and answer questions.
numbers: Best agent (task-specific CORE-Agent): 60% on the easiest level, 21% on the hardest. Tested AutoGPT and CORE-Agent with GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini.
limits: CodeOcean capsules; three difficulty levels; hardware limits.
agent_relevance: Even rerunning supplied code is hard for agents at the hard level. Run-and-compare steps need explicit program support.

source: Siegel et al. (2024) CORE-Bench: fostering the credibility of published research through a computational reproducibility agent benchmark
finding: The paper tabulates computational reproducibility failures across 15 fields even when code and data are shared.
numbers: Table 1 lists two counts per study, e.g. Economics 203 and 128 (Gertler 2018), Psychology 25 and 16 (Hardwicke 2021), Medicine 17 and 3 (Naudet 2018), ML 28 and 10 (Sinha 2023). Column labels garbled in extraction.
limits: Column meaning inferred as studies reviewed and studies reproduced; verify against the PDF before quoting.
agent_relevance: Shared code and data are not enough. Rerun stability is a check in its own right.
